subject: St Martin of Tours: the miracles section (draft, 2026-09-24)
text_used: Alexander Roberts (tr.), Sulpitius Severus, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), CCEL plain text, the same copy martin-facts.json checked against. Roberts's Dialogues are three (I, II, III). 'quote' must be a verbatim substring of that text, footnote numbers removed.

intro.text: Sulpicius tells dozens of wonders. He knew they would be doubted, and he made a promise at the start of the Life.
intro.quote: I implore those who are to read what follows to give full faith to the things narrated, and to believe that I have written nothing of which I had not certain knowledge and evidence.

raised.title: The catechumen
raised.text: A catechumen had joined Martin's monastery. He died of a fever while Martin was away, before he could be baptised. Martin sent everyone out, lay down on the body and prayed. Within about two hours the man began to move. He was baptised and lived for many years.
raised.quote: they beheld the man alive whom they had formerly left dead
raised.witness: The man told the story himself. He said he had stood before God's judgment, until two angels said he was the man Martin was praying for.

raised.title: The slave
raised.text: Passing the estate of Lupicinus, a man of high standing, Martin found a crowd wailing. One of the household's slaves had hanged himself. Martin went in alone, lay on the body and prayed. The dead man woke, took Martin's right hand and stood up. Then he walked with Martin to the porch, in front of everyone.
raised.quote: with life beaming in his countenance, and with his drooping eyes fixed on Martin's face
raised.witness: The whole crowd saw him walk out, says Sulpicius.

raised.title: The only son
raised.text: They passed a village where no one knew a single Christian, and a huge crowd of pagans came out to meet him. A mother held up her dead son and begged him. Martin took the body in his arms, knelt and prayed, and gave the child back to her alive. The crowd asked to become Christians on the spot, and he made them all catechumens there in the plain.
raised.quote: We know that you are a friend of God: restore me my son, who is my only one.
raised.witness: Gallus, his disciple, was there: “I myself am a witness to this latter occurrence”.

raised_note.text: Martin used to tell Sulpicius that as a bishop he had less power to work wonders than he had before.
raised_note.quote: such an abundance of power was by no means granted him while he was a bishop, as he remembered to have possessed before he obtained that office

more.title: The falling pine
more.text: Martin had torn down a village's old temple, and he meant to cut down the sacred pine beside it. The pagans made him a deal: they would cut it down themselves if he stood where it fell. They bound him and set him where it would fall. As the tree came down, he raised his hand and made the sign of the cross. It swung round and fell the other way. Almost the whole crowd asked to become Christians that day.
more.quote: it swept round to the opposite side, to such a degree that it almost crushed the rustics

more.title: The leper at Paris
more.text: At the gate of Paris, with crowds around him, Martin kissed a leper and blessed him. The man was cleansed. The next day he came to church with healthy skin to give thanks.
more.quote: he gave a kiss to a leper, of miserable appearance, while all shuddered at seeing him do so

more.title: Paulinus's eye
more.text: Paulinus, later the famous bishop of Nola, had a thick skin growing over the pupil of one eye, and it hurt badly. Martin touched it with a paintbrush, and the pain went and the eye was healed.
more.quote: Martin touched his eye with a painter's brush

more.title: A globe of fire
more.text: On a great feast day, as Martin blessed the altar, a ball of fire rose from his head, trailing a long flame. The church was crowded, but only five people saw it: one consecrated virgin, one priest and three monks.
more.quote: we beheld a globe of fire dart from his head

doubters.text: Doubters came early. A friend told Sulpicius of one man who said he had “told many lies in that book of yours”. In the last Dialogue, Gallus says many doubted what he had told the day before. So from then on he names living witnesses, people a doubter could go and ask.
doubters.quote_1: told many lies in that book of yours
doubters.quote_2: if any one is inclined to disbelieve, he may have recourse, because they are still in the body

stats_added.label: Raised the dead
lines: Two as a monk, one as bishop
stats_added.cite: Life of St Martin, chapters 7 and 8; Dialogue II, chapter 4

stats_added.label: Monks at his funeral
lines: Almost two thousand, it was said
stats_added.quote: They are said to have assembled on that day almost to the number of two thousand

checked.how: One adversarial checker read every retelling against Roberts's text and the Latin (Halm's Life at The Latin Library; the Dialogues on Latin Wikisource, Migne PL 20), and fetched every URL (all 200, right heading). Every quotation is word for word. Six fixes applied: Lupicinus 'of high standing', not rich (honorati secundum saeculum viri); the only son 'on the road to Chartres', not near it, and not 'a whole village'; the raised-note is about wonders in general (virtutum gratiam), said to Sulpicius; at the pine he was 'bound' and set on the spot (vinctus statuitur), not tied to it; the doubters note names the right speakers (Postumianus in Dialogue I.26 reports what he heard; Gallus in Dialogue III.5 answers doubts about his own stories of the day before).

open_items_resolved.martyrology: 1916 Roman Martyrology p. 347, exact: 'At Tours, in France, the birthday of blessed Martin, bishop and confessor, whose life was so renowned for miracles that he received the power to raise three persons from the dead.' Its own footnote on p. 2: 'In the language of the Church, birthday refers to the day on which a Saint enters heaven.' (https://archive.org/stream/romanmartyrology00cathuoft/romanmartyrology00cathuoft_djvu.txt)
